title: The Firmament and the Shape of the World
lead: How the Bible pictures the world: a sky God spread out like a tent or hammered out like metal, waters above it, an earth set on bases and pillars, and the round line of the horizon. Readers differ on whether this is the world described as it looks to us, an ancient picture that God spoke within, or a hint of modern science. On every reading the point is the same: God made it all, and nothing holds it up but him.

sections.h: The dome and the waters above
sections.b: On the second day God makes a raqia', which the Plain calls a "dome," and "he divided the waters under the dome from the waters above the dome" (Genesis 1:7). The related verb raqa' means to hammer or beat out: it is used for gold beaten into thin plates (Exodus 39:3) and for bronze censers beaten into a covering for the altar (Numbers 16:39). Elihu asks Job whether he can "join him in hammering out the skies, / hard as a mirror cast from metal" (Job 37:18). The Greek translators wrote stereōma, "something firm," and Jerome's Latin firmamentum, which gave the KJV its word "firmament." A psalm calls on "you waters over the heavens" to praise God (Psalm 148:4); other passages speak of "the windows of the sky" that open and shut at the flood (Genesis 7:11; Genesis 8:2), and of a dome "shining like awesome ice" above the living creatures in Ezekiel's vision (Ezekiel 1:22). Yet the same Bible also pictures the sky as cloth: God "stretches the heavens out like a thin veil" (Isaiah 40:22) and spreads them "like a tent curtain" (Psalm 104:2).

sections.h: Bases, pillars, and an earth hung on nothing
sections.b:
Hannah sings, "The earth's pillars belong to the LORD, / and he has set the world on them" (1 Samuel 2:8). God says, "I myself have made its pillars firm" (Psalm 75:3), and asks Job, "Into what were its bases sunk? / Who set down its corner stone" (Job 38:6). When God shakes the world, "the pillars under it shudder" (Job 9:6). But Job also says, "on nothing at all he hangs the earth" (Job 26:7): the Hebrew belimah means "without anything," and the Greek has "on nothing."

"He is seated high over the circle of the earth" (Isaiah 40:22). The Hebrew chug is a circle drawn on a surface, the same word used when God "carved a circle on the surface of the deep" (Proverbs 8:27) and "traced a ring across the surface of the waters" (Job 26:10); the Greek has gyros, "a ring." Isaiah knew a word for a ball, dur (Isaiah 22:18), and does not use it here. So the verse proves neither a flat disk nor a globe: it pictures God enthroned above the round horizon. In the same way, "the four corners of the earth" (Revelation 7:1; Isaiah 11:12) is a way of saying "everywhere," as English speakers still say "the four corners of the globe."

sections.b:
An ancient picture God spoke within. Paul Seely argues that the raqia' "was originally conceived of as being solid," a real dome holding back water, and that most ancient Jews and Christians read it that way. Standard Hebrew dictionaries and a number of modern scholars agree (Seely names Driver, Gunkel, Skinner, von Rad and Westermann). Seely, who still calls the verse "infallibly true," concludes that it is not the purpose of Genesis 1:7 "to teach us the physical nature of the sky, but to reveal the creator of the sky." He quotes B. B. Warfield, who allowed that an inspired writer might "share the ordinary opinions of his day" on matters such as "the form of the earth."

The world as it looks. Calvin held that in Genesis 1 "nothing is here treated of but the visible form of the world," took the waters above to be the clouds, and wrote, "He who would learn astronomy, and other recondite arts, let him go elsewhere." Seely notes that many conservative commentators after Calvin, such as Keil and Delitzsch, read raqia' as the open sky or atmosphere. The Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978, Article XIII) says the Bible's truth is not undone by "observational descriptions of nature."

A hint of later science. Some readers take Job 26:7 as knowledge ahead of its time. Ray Comfort, in Scientific Facts in the Bible (2016), writes that "The Bible proclaims that the earth freely floats in space." Others answer that the same books also speak of pillars and bases, that erets here may mean the land rather than the planet, and that poetry is not a lesson in geography.

Not a flat-earth church. It is a common mistake to think the church once taught a flat earth. Augustine, in The City of God (16.9), granted that the world may be "of a round and spherical form"; he only doubted that people lived on the far side. The rabbis, too, could learn from outsiders: in the Talmud, when the sages of Israel and the sages of the nations disagreed about where the sun goes at night, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said the other sages' view "appears to be more accurate than our statement" (Pesachim 94b).
